budget_items.topic: State open space grant funding eligibility
budget_items.what_was_said: Brandon stressed that the main value of keeping the open space plan current is that it keeps the town eligible for state grant funding not otherwise available to municipalities, calling it a light lift for a real future benefit.

decisions.decision: Brandon announced he is resigning from the Open Space Committee effective after this meeting and will send a resignation letter to the planning board (the committee's oversight board).
Tim Lawless, the parks commission's representative to the committee, is also stepping aside, creating another vacancy.
Committee will look at moving its June meeting to Monday, June 9th to coincide with the planning board's meeting, pending quorum.
Chair (Mike) will take the lead on updating the open space plan's action-item table from a 7-year to a 10-year format to secure a 3-year extension (to 2029) from the state.
Before sending the updated plan to the state, it will be circulated to the planning board, parks commission, agricultural commission, conservation commission, town manager and select board for input.
July meeting will remain on its usual date, the second Wednesday of July.

what_happened.line: A longtime committee member and the parks commission's representative both announced they are stepping down, opening several vacancies.
The committee moved to seek a three-year extension of the open space plan to 2029 by updating its state action-item table.
Before submission, the updated plan will circulate to the planning board, parks, agricultural and conservation commissions, the town manager and the select board.
The committee discussed tightening the six criteria used to evaluate right-of-first-refusal properties, without resolving changes.

why_it_matters: The plan extension keeps the town eligible for state open space grant funding not otherwise open to municipalities.
Two vacancies, including the parks commission's seat, reduce the committee's membership as it takes on this state filing.
Any tightening of right-of-first-refusal criteria would change how the town screens land offered to it before a private sale.
